examples: When I heard the news that I had passed, I was happier than words can say.
His attentiveness to others is beyond words.
This road is unbelievably dark. It's too dangerous to walk on.
The traffic jam is terrible beyond words.
I am more grateful than I can say that you helped me.
fields.explain:
Can be used in polite contexts and in writing that describes emotions/impressions.
To emphasize a strong subjective emotion, it can stand as an independent sentence: きれい といったらない。
With nouns, prefer Nの/Aさ for naturalness: 美しさ といったらない rather than 美しい といったらない in some contexts.

- Expresses an extremely high degree, “very / beyond description”; more neutral than ありはしない/ありゃしない. Can be used for both praise and criticism; suits written language and polite speech.
• Focuses on describing intensity, with little nuance of crude complaint.
• Often used with emotions/abstract qualities: 嬉しさ・ありがたさ・美しさ・恥ずかしさ・迷惑…
• ほど/くらい can be added to express the degree more softly.
fields.notes:
• Literal meaning “there is nothing more to say (describe)” → figurative “indescribable”.
• When it follows a long clause, nominalize it for coherence: 〜という事実の重大さといったらない。
• Often appears in descriptive writing, reportage and accounts of emotions.
mistakes: Using it directly with the dictionary form of a verb → unnatural. Use a nominalization instead: 驚きといったらない／疲れといったらない.
Confusing its nuance with ありはしない/ありゃしない: exam questions test politeness/neutrality.
Using it for objective facts that require absolute objectivity (scientific writing) → avoid; choose “非常に/極めて”.
Repeating the adjective: “とても嬉しいといったらない” is redundant emphasis; the JLPT often sets an “over-emphasis” trap.

examples: When it comes to my boss, he always shows up late to meetings.
That dog next door does nothing but bark in the middle of the night. It's a real nuisance.
The weather lately — just when you think it's cleared up, it starts raining again.
That restaurant — the food is good, but the service is terrible.
My little brother forgets his promises in no time.
fields.explain:
Used like “speaking of …”, but leans toward criticism/blame; avoid using it about superiors in formal situations.
Often paired with casual sentence endings: ～んだ、～ったらない、～こと！
Not used for formal praise; to praise, use another pattern.

• Introduces a topic in order to criticize, complain about, or express surprise in a negative direction about the target N.
• Used often in conversation; not suitable in formal documents or when talking about the listener (it can sound rude).
• Usually followed by concrete examples of bad habits, shortcomings or repeated trouble.
fields.notes:
• Can be used to open a story of complaint and catch the listener's attention.
• Talking directly about the listener can easily seem impolite; replacing it with ね or やっぱり… sounds softer.
• To further emphasize the degree of the complaint, continue with ～ったらない／～ことだ。
mistakes: Using it in a formal style/academic paper → inappropriate.
It can be used about yourself as self-criticism, but avoid being rude to the listener/superiors.
Confusing it with といったら（degree） in JLPT questions: check whether the second clause is a “complaint” → choose ときたら.

rows: Strongly colloquial, very casual; ときたら is slightly more formal.
<ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>ってば、また<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れたの？
Neutral, for information/explanation; implies no criticism.
<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>については<ruby>後<rt>のち</rt></ruby>ほど。
A pattern of degree, often used with ～ない/～たらない; a different function.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>食欲<rt>しょくよく</rt></ruby>といったらすごい。

fields.connection: V plain form + ときている / N / Na / Aい + い
examples: It's cheap and delicious on top of that, so there's no way it wouldn't draw a line.
He's smart and a hard worker as well, so it's only natural that he gets results.
The deadline is close, and on top of that we're short-staffed. Overtime is unavoidable.
It's convenient, and yet the rent is surprisingly cheap.
It's raining from the very first day, so we'll have to rework our plans.
fields.explain:
Has the nuance “no wonder / and on top of that” → exclamation with evaluation.
Suited to presenting an obvious reason that leads to a consequence: …わけだ／当然だ／無理はない／〜に決まっている.
Can be used for both praise and criticism; often used when piling up several favorable/unfavorable conditions.

- Presents a feature/circumstance as “and on top of that…”, indicating that it is a very favorable/unfavorable condition leading to an understandable consequence. Carries an exclamatory nuance, sometimes sarcasm, complaint or admiration.
• Often lists 2+ strengths/weaknesses and then concludes “no wonder…”.
• Used with から/ので/ものだから/のに to connect to the consequence.
• Mainly with N/Adj or state phrases (Aくて/Bで/Cも… + ときている).
fields.notes:
• The form “Xときているから/ので” is the typical frame: state X (a striking condition) → an obvious conclusion.
• Easily combined with listing: AくてBでCときている (piling up conditions).
• Often used in commentary on daily life/consumption/the economy: 値段・立地・性能・人手・天候…
mistakes: Attaching it directly to a pure action clause that does not express a “quality”: use a quality/state instead. Incorrect) 彼が来るときている → Correct) 彼が有名人ときている／忙しいときている.
Confusing it with “ときたら” (a pattern for criticizing a topic) → a different function; the JLPT often tests this pair.
Leaving out the concluding consequence → the sentence feels incomplete. This pattern usually leads to a conclusion like “no wonder / naturally…”.
Mistaking its nuance for objective: the pattern is exclamatory; in strictly serious writing, switch to “ため/ので”.

examples: 「Thank you very much for taking the trouble to come when you are so busy.」
「Excuse me for interrupting your conversation.」
「I'm very sorry to call you so early in the morning while you're resting.」
I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy, but please sign here.
Just as we were about to start the meeting, a call came in from the company president.
I'm truly sorry for waking you up while you were sleeping.
fields.explain:
When used to apologize/make a request: it comes at the beginning of the sentence, followed by a short, polite request. Often accompanied by 恐れ入ります／失礼します／申し訳ありません.
In the meaning of “concession”: the preceding clause (before ところを) states an unfavorable condition / what should have happened, and the second clause shows a result contrary to expectations (leniency, letting it go, helping anyway...)
Used with verbs of perception/control: 見る／見つける／撮る／捕まえる to emphasize the exact point in time of being discovered/caught.
More formal than 〜のに. Avoid overusing it in casual conversation (it can sound affected).

• Meaning 1: Indicates the exact point in time when an action takes place. Emphasizes “right at that moment” (in progress / just done / about to). It depends on the form of ところ:

- V-るところ: about to, getting ready to

- V-ているところ: in the middle of

- V-たところ: have just

• Meaning 2: Politeness/apology when intruding on the other person's situation. Pattern: お忙しいところを／お休みのところを／夜分のところを + 失礼します など.
• Meaning 3: Formal concession “although / should have”. Used when handing down a lenient decision, thanking, or apologizing:

例: 厳しく叱るべきところを、温かい言葉をいただいた。
• Nuance: More formal than ところで/のに. In the concessive meaning, it is often seen in official documents, minutes and speeches.
fields.notes:
• The “place – point in time” sense of ところ frames the situation, making an apology/request softer and showing awareness of the inconvenience caused.
• In minutes/decisions, ところを often goes with the passive form/honorific language to increase formality.
• V-たところを in the time sense is often equivalent to “had just … when”, creating a sense of surprise.
mistakes: Confusing it with ところで: ところを carries a nuance of apology/concession or indicates the point in time of being affected; ところで usually means “by the way, even if”.
Wrong tense/form: when apologizing while the other person “is” doing something → use V-ているところを, not V-るところを.
Too casual a use: in conversation with friends, ところを can sound a bit stiff; replace it with のに／ときは…など.

JLPT: trick questions often use inversion of the clauses to test your understanding of the concession “should have … but …”. Note that the preceding clause (before ところを) states “what should/ought to happen”.

fields.connection: V plain form + とはいえ / N + (だ) / Na + (だ) / Aい + い
examples: It may be spring, but the nights are still cold.
You may be new, but you will still have to follow the basics.
Although I've lived in Japan for a long time, keigo is still difficult for me.
It may be cheap, but I don't want to buy things I don't need.
They may be experts, but even they can't reduce mistakes to zero.
fields.explain:
Used to “soften, then counter”: acknowledges A but emphasizes that B is the main point.
Serious style, suited to reports, arguments and news.
Often used with words that limit the degree: まだ、やはり、必ずしも、それでも.
Different from にしては: とはいえ does not compare against a specific standard, but simply concedes and then counters.

• A pattern of concession/acceptance of fact A, while the second clause B gives a judgment contrary to expectations: “although… still…”.
• Formal nuance, written language; stronger than けど/が; close to とはいえ＝とは言え.
• The second clause is usually an evaluation, a limitation or a counterargument: with the feel of しかし/それでも/とはいっても.
• Not followed directly by an opposing command/volition; usually by a judgment or an objective fact.
fields.notes:
• Both the full form とは言え (kanji) and とはいえ (kana) are used; kana is more common today.
• Often combined with nouns of time/season: 春・子どもの日・連休 とはいえ,...
• Can stand in the middle of a sentence or at the beginning of a sentence to open a counterargument: とはいえ、～。
• With the past: ～たとはいえ emphasizes “although … already …, still …”.
mistakes: Confusing it with にしては: とはいえ has no specific standard of comparison; if there is a clear standard (年齢のわりに), use にしては.
Following とはいえ with a direct command sounds harsh; use a judgment/comment instead.
Nuance trap: といっても leans toward the colloquial; とはいえ is formal. Choose according to the context.
JLPT: when a sentence needs “acknowledge A but hold position B”, the answer is usually とはいえ/とはいうものの.

rows: <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いとはいえ、<ruby>質<rt>しつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>だ。
Plays down the degree of A, more colloquial
<ruby>金持<rt>かねも</rt></ruby>ちといっても、<ruby>普通<rt>ふつう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>だ。
Compared with the standard of A...
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもにしては、<ruby>字<rt>じ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>上手<rt>じょうず</rt></ruby>だ。
Written language, formal, similar meaning; とはいうものの is stronger
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>したものの、<ruby>不安<rt>ふあん</rt></ruby>だ。

examples: There's no comparison between today's smartphones and those of ten years ago.
His performance this time was so superb that there's no comparing it with last time.
This shop's service is in a completely different class from other shops.
Prices in the city are incomparably higher than in the countryside.
Amateur work can't compare with that of professionals.
fields.explain:
Typical structure: AはBとは比べものにならない（A far surpasses/falls far short of B）. The topic is usually A.
Often combined with ほど／くらい to emphasize the degree: ～ほど速い／～くらい高い.
Decisive tone; suited to commentary, evaluation, and comparing products/performance.

• Expresses a gap so large that comparison becomes meaningless: “cannot be compared with …”.
• Usually used for praise/superiority (A is better than B), but can also criticize (A is far worse than B) depending on the context.
• More formal than くらいじゃない/桁違いだ; usable in writing and presentations.
fields.notes:
• “とは” marks the point of comparison. In colloquial speech it can be replaced with “と(は)”: ～とは／～と(は)比べものにならない.
• Easy to use in headlines/commentary: コスパは前機種とは比べものにならない.
• To stay neutral, ～より（も） is better than this absolute negation.
mistakes: Reversing A/B causes misunderstanding: topic A is what is evaluated against B.
Using it in contexts that call for objectivity or an indirect expression: avoid it, as it is too absolute.
Confusing it with ～に匹敵する (equivalent) in trick questions: watch for keywords like “surpass / far different”.

rows: Usually means “not at that level”; a different function from direct comparison.
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しくて<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>どころではない。
Strongly colloquial; less formal than <ruby>比<rt>くら</rt></ruby>べものにならない.
<ruby>性能<rt>せいのう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>桁違<rt>けたちが</rt></ruby>いだ。
Means being equal (positive); pragmatically the opposite of “cannot compare”.
<ruby>世界<rt>せかい</rt></ruby><ruby>記録<rt>きろく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>匹敵<rt>ひってき</rt></ruby>する。
Short and colloquial; similar nuance but abbreviated.

examples: Expensive things are not necessarily good.
Not all Japanese people like sushi.
Just because it's raining doesn't mean the match will be canceled.
Information online is not always accurate.
Having long experience doesn't necessarily mean you can get results.
This station has been sung about for a long time, but that doesn't mean every Japanese person knows it.
fields.explain:
Objective, polite nuance; often used in debate, academic writing and news.
Placed after a clause regarded as a common assumption/stereotype to negate its absoluteness.
Add 必ずしも to emphasize “not necessarily”.
The combination “Aからといって、Bとは限らない” is a very natural frame.

• Not necessarily / not always ~; negates inevitability/generality.
• Often used with 必ずしも for emphasis: 必ずしも～とは限らない.
• Used to refute stereotypes/generalizations: “if A, then B” is not always true.
fields.notes:
• Often appears in counterarguments: AからといってBとは限らない.
• To soften the negation, いつも/必ずしも/必然的に + ～とは限らない can be added.
• Suitable when you want to allow for exceptions and avoid absolute assertions. meaning_vi: not necessarily ～, not certain that ～ ⏐ explain: Used for partial negation of things and events. ⏐ examples: 1. 相手が弱いチームであっても、必ず勝つとは限らない。
Even if the opponent is a weak team, you can't necessarily win easily.
2. あまり使わない表現だが、必ずしもテストに出ないとは限らない。
It's a rarely used expression, but that doesn't mean it won't appear on the test.
mistakes: Dropping は in とは限らない: × という限らない → 〇 とは限らない.
Confusing it with absolute negation: ～とは限らない only allows for exceptions; it does not negate completely.
Forgetting だ with N/na in written language: 学生だとは限らない.
JLPT trap: choose the correct pair “必ずしも～とは限らない” rather than “必ず～ない”.

fields.connection: V plain form + とみると
examples: Whenever my older brother sees a sale, he buys things in bulk.
As soon as the children saw that the teacher wasn't there, they started making a racket.
The moment the cat saw the door open slightly, it darted outside.
As soon as the enemy saw that we were tired, they attacked all at once.
Whenever he sees an opportunity, he gets in touch right away.
fields.explain:
Has a narrative nuance, describing a quick reaction, with a touch of surprise or establishing a habit.
Unnatural if followed by a command/the speaker's direct volition (let's / go on…). Suited to description, not to making requests.
Often used with words that suggest a “signal”: チャンス、セール、隙、警官の姿、雨雲…

• Used when, “having just noticed/judged that it is X”, action Y occurs “immediately/regularly”. Emphasizes a quick reflex or a habit.
• The subject of the second clause is usually someone else/the target being described; the speaker narrates the situation.
• Can express a regular pattern: “Whenever X is seen, Y” (habit). Also used for one specific instance (causing surprise).
fields.notes:
• Use the past to narrate a one-time event: ～たとみると、～た。
• The first clause can be the subjective evaluation of the subject in the sentence: 敵は我々が弱いとみると…
• Easily used with adverbials of immediacy: すぐ／途端に／一気に／さっと…
mistakes: Using it to give a direct command/advice in the second clause → unnatural: × 安いとみると、買いましょう！
Confusing it with ～たとたん: ～とみると has a nuance of “judging, then reacting”, not just a point in time.
Using it for purely internal emotions that are hard to observe → inappropriate: × 悲しいとみると、泣いた (use ～とたん if it is about a point in time).

rows: As soon as X is noticed, Y
Formal, means an instant point in time
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>した。

examples: Depending on the conditions, it's not out of the question that we would accept.
If it's just a little, I could possibly help.
If you make an effort, it's not impossible to pass.
Once you get used to it, this design might not be so bad after all.
Depending on the price, I might buy it.
fields.explain:
Nuance of an “indirect expression”: no strong commitment; shows openness, but with conditions.
Often accompanied by conditions: ～ば／～なら／条件次第で／工夫すれば／少しなら.
Suited to negotiations, discussions, and polite answers that do not bind you.

• “It's not that … not…”, “It is possible…/it's not entirely impossible…”.
• Weak, reserved affirmation, often with conditions or exceptions.
• Used to open the way to negotiation, expressing possible acceptance under certain conditions.
fields.notes:
• Suitable when you want to keep a “safety margin” in what you say and avoid absolute commitment.
• In work emails: 前向きに検討しないものでもない（considering it positively but not promising yet).
• Apart from verbs, with adjectives it is usually the fixed phrase “悪くないものでもない”.
mistakes: Using it as a firm promise → wrong nuance: this is only weak, conditional acceptance.
Confusing it with ～ないものだろうか (wish). Here it is about “possibility/conditional agreement”, not “wishing”.
Leaving out the condition makes the sentence vague: adding “～ば／～なら／次第で” makes the meaning clear.
The JLPT often asks you to distinguish ないことはない／なくはない／ないものでもない by their degree of reserve.
